## 1.1 The essay, claim by claim

The source is `essay_transcription.md` in the project files, twenty-six handwritten pages. Read in order, the argument builds in six moves.

**Move 1: Every invention trades a skill for ease, and that is usually fine.**

Your opening is deliberately not anti-technology. You write that humans discovered fire by rubbing two stones, then developed better tools, and "maybe we forgot those ancient methods to make fire from the fundamentals, but we still hold the fundamentals." The word doing the work is *fundamentals*. The trade is acceptable when the underlying capability survives the convenience.

This matters more than it looks. It is the reason the project is not a Luddite argument, and it is why the eventual design is a mirror and not a blocker. You are not against the tool. You are against a specific kind of loss.

**Move 2: There was a turn, and it is datable.**

You divide history at a line. Printing press, agricultural revolution, industrial revolution: these were inventions "to prosper and make humans more productive." Then, "now all the inventions are mostly geared towards the capitalistic gains, not for a real productive human advancement."

The pivot example is Google Maps. Before it, people navigated, watched their surroundings, remembered routes. After it, "we are stuck without the map and not confident on this skill."

**Move 3: The design intent is dependence, not help.**

Page 4 is the sharpest page in the essay. You argue these tools are "designed, marketed in such a fascinating way to make people only believe and confident when they know they have Google Maps." And then the observation the entire project rests on:

> "If they don't have phone or it gets switched off, people panic. They believe they cannot solve what they already had, and the truth is they still have it within them, they just forgot it."

Read that twice. The loss you identified is not the skill. The skill is still present. What was lost is the *belief* that the skill is present. That distinction is the whole thesis.

**Move 4: AI is this pattern applied to thinking itself.**

Your examples are concrete and personal: a boombox that needs fixing, so you photograph it and ask Claude. A website you want, so you ask AI to build it. Ingredients in the fridge, so you ask what to cook. In each case, you write, it "entirely skips the whole process of our own thinking."

The cooking example is the one that carries the most weight, because you follow it through: before AI, a person hunts for an old recipe, improvises, gets it wrong, and in the process invents something that comes "from the wisdom of the places." That invention is what gets skipped.

**Move 5: Scale turns individual convenience into collective flattening.**

"A billion people asking AI" means a billion answers drawn from the average of everything already on the internet. You write that "everything will be the average of it." Not that any single answer is bad. That the distribution of human outputs collapses toward the centre.

Your two worked examples are the 2019 portfolio website and the filmmaker. The filmmaker one is the more revealing. You describe the child who has a wild imaginative idea, then learns it is hard, then constructs a simpler version he can actually pull off, and grows through that constraint. Then the AI version: he has the idea, goes straight to AI, and "does not talk with the cameraman with vision, technician with editing skills, actors with their own imagination." The loss is not just his own thinking. It is every other mind that would have touched the idea and changed it.

**Move 6: The remedy is awareness, not prohibition.**

The closing pages are all imperative. "AI giving you a solution is not the only way of solving." "It is always not necessary that we should save time, time is an illusion." "Pause, think, figure out, action." And in capitals, page 24:

## 1.4 The four ideas, and what happened to each

**Idea 1: the Pause / Blocker layer.** A layer between you and any AI tool that interrupts before a chat: do you really need AI for this? It would identify whether you are in Cyborg, Centaur or Self-Automator mode and offer alternatives.

This is the essay's own closing proposal, turned into a product. You killed it yourself, and the reasoning was correct: it is a blocker, people bypass blockers, it adds cost with no payoff, and it is a nag rather than a design. It preaches to people who did not ask to be preached at.

What survived: the conviction that AI interaction is too frictionless, and that a *designed* pause has value. The conviction survived. The nagging mechanism did not.

**Idea 2: the Generation-Wait Canvas.** While an AI image generates, the loading window is replaced by a drawing canvas. You sketch a rough prediction of the image you are about to receive. Generation continues in the background. Then you reveal and compare your sketch against the result.

Three threads were fused here: prediction (sketch before reveal), attention tethering (stay in the task instead of reaching for your phone), and competence (keep exercising your own imagination).

This one was never formally killed, and you should know that. The prior assessment was blunt about it: most buildable, most demonstrable, most original in framing, and the comparison step already embodies the "make the human's contribution visible" thesis. Its weaknesses were that the claim about drawing skill is soft (it is imaginative competence, not drawing competence), it breaks when a reference image is supplied because there is no gap left to predict, and the generation wait window keeps shrinking as models get faster.

It is a live fallback. Not a recommendation, just a fact you should carry.

**Idea 3: the LLM mind-map / journey tracker.** A live map of a conversation so you can navigate it instead of re-reading, see turning points, see who decided what.

Killed for a specific reason: the "navigate your chat as a tree" half is saturated. There are shipping browser extensions for it across ChatGPT, Gemini and DeepSeek, plus branching apps. Do not rebuild it.

One fragment survived, and it became the next idea: *decision attribution*. Who decided what.

**Idea 4: the Contribution / Agency Chat-Map.** The committed idea. From your handwritten note:

> An LLM chatbot with an integrated side-panel timeline that helps users keep track of the entire AI conversation. A collapsible timeline on the right side shows, at a high level via red and blue lines, the contribution split: what the user gave versus the micro-decisions the AI made. Clicking a level expands what was user-given versus AI-directed. After each prompt the user can add a label, bookmark, turning point or decision marker. At the end, the user can see how the whole collaboration went, on which occasions direct and indirect influence occurred, so that the user has full clarity at all times on who held the upper agency, and can identify how much they actually participated.

That is the origin statement. It has evolved considerably since, and Step 3 covers what it is now. Note two things in the original that are worth tracking: the user-placed markers, and the phrase *upper agency*.

## 2.0 The four layers, and what each one is for

| Layer | Question it answers | Job in the thesis |

## 2.1 Layer 1: the problem is empirically real

Your essay was written from observation. These studies say the observation holds up. Four clusters.

**Cognitive offloading reduces critical thinking.**

- **Gerlich (2025), SBS Swiss Business School**, published in *Societies*. 666 participants. Found a significant negative correlation between AI tool use and critical thinking, mediated by cognitive offloading. The effect was strongest in ages 17 to 25. That age detail matters for your framing: the people least equipped to notice the loss are the ones experiencing it most.
- **Lee et al. (2025), Microsoft Research with Carnegie Mellon.** 319 knowledge workers, 936 real tasks. Two findings worth memorising. Higher confidence in AI predicts *less* critical thinking; higher confidence in oneself predicts *more*. And workers refrain from critical thinking precisely when they lack the skills to inspect the AI's output, which is a vicious circle. They coined the term **mechanised convergence** for the narrowing of outcomes.
- **Kosmyna et al. (2025), MIT Media Lab, "Your Brain on ChatGPT."** EEG study, 54 participants writing essays. The ChatGPT group showed the weakest neural connectivity and produced homogeneous essays that reviewers described as soulless. By the third essay, participants were largely pasting. Their term is **cognitive debt**, and the important part is that the atrophy persisted after the tool was removed.

**The Google Maps example is neurologically real.** The McGill Bohbot lab (2010, plus a 2020 longitudinal study in *Scientific Reports*) found habitual GPS users show measurable hippocampal atrophy, with more lifetime GPS use predicting steeper decline in spatial memory. Reverse causation was ruled out. The counterpart is the London taxi driver studies showing enlarged hippocampi. Your essay's central metaphor is not a metaphor.

**The "average of everything" claim has four supporting papers.**

- **Doshi and Hauser (2024), *Science Advances*.** Generative AI made individual stories more creative but collectively more similar. Net diversity decreased. This is your essay's argument proven with a clean experimental design, and it is the single best citation you have for the scale argument.
- **Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024)**, "Homogenization Effects of LLMs on Human Creative Ideation."
- **Peterson (2024)**, "AI and the Problem of Knowledge Collapse," in *AI & Society*. Formalises the narrowing: LLMs generate from the centre of the distribution, and the long tail gets progressively forgotten.
- **Jiang et al. (2025), "Artificial Hivemind"** (UW, CMU, AI2). Different LLMs converge on near-identical phrasing, so switching providers does not restore diversity.

**What this layer buys you:** you can assert every claim in Step 1's essay without hedging, with a named study behind each one. Cluster one covers the skill loss. The McGill work covers the confidence loss. Cluster three covers the homogenisation.

## 2.2 Layer 2: the BCG archetypes, and the empty quadrant

This is the course's own vocabulary, from the BCG paper by Randazzo et al. that sits in your project files.

Three archetypes:

- **Centaur** (Directed Co-Creation): a clean division of labour. The human decides, the AI executes on request. Outcome: **upskilling**.
- **Cyborg** (Fused Co-Creation): human and AI interleave continuously, each shaping the other's moves in real time. Outcome: **newskilling**, meaning new capabilities that neither party had alone.
- **Self-Automator** (Abdicated Co-Creation): the human hands over the task and receives the result. Outcome: **no skilling**. This is the danger zone, and it is the archetype your essay is about.

The structural insight, worked out in an earlier session, is what makes this more than a set of labels. **BCG's framework has two axes: who decides *what*, and who decides *how*.** That maps directly onto COTRACE's two roles, SHAPER and EXECUTOR. So the two papers are not two separate frameworks. The BCG archetypes are the macro pattern; COTRACE's action-level labels are the micro mechanics that add up to them.

That mapping is why the panel has a WHAT axis and a HOW axis, and it is the strongest piece of theoretical scaffolding the project has.

The second insight is the **empty fourth quadrant**. If the two axes are who decides what and who decides how, there are four cells, but BCG only names three. The unnamed one is: *AI decides what, human executes how*. Nobody named it because nobody thinks they are in it. That quadrant is precisely the blind spot COTRACE's indirect influence tracing was built to expose, and it is arguably the most interesting territory in the whole project.

Alongside this sits the German framework from **Weßels and Maibaum, "Vom Deskilling zum Newskilling"** (pages 01 to 03 in your project files): Reskilling, Upskilling, Skill Skipping, No Skilling, Deskilling. Skill Skipping is the one that adds something BCG lacks, because it names the case where the shortcut bypasses learning that would have happened.

## 2.3 Layer 3: COTRACE, the key paper

**"I Didn't Make the Micro Decisions": Measuring, Inducing, and Exposing Goal-Level AI Contributions in Collaboration.** Eunsu Kim (KAIST), Jessica R. Mindel (CMU), Kyungjin Kim (SNU), Sherry Tongshuang Wu (CMU). arXiv 2605.21363, May 2026. Code at github.com/rladmstn1714/CoTrace. The PDF is in your project files as `Measuring_AI_Contributions.pdf`, packaged as a layered export.

This is the paper the entire technical half of your project is built on. Four parts to understand.

### The framework

COTRACE is a **goal-level attribution** framework. Rather than asking who wrote which words, it asks who shaped which goals.

- Goals decompose into a hierarchy: **parent goals → child goals → requirements**, where a requirement is the smallest verifiable success predicate. Something that can be checked true or false against the output.
- Two kinds of influence. **Direct goal shaping** is when an action explicitly introduces or modifies a requirement. **Indirect influence** is when an action supplies context that later motivates a requirement. The second is the hard, novel part.
- Two roles per action. **SHAPER** proposes goals, ideas, requirements. **EXECUTOR** carries out and produces output.

### The pipeline

Four stages, and these are the stages your own engine reimplements:

1. **Outcome and action extraction.** Break each turn into atomic actions, tag each with a role.
2. **Requirement extraction.** Pull the binary-testable success conditions out of the conversation.
3. **Influence labelling.** For every requirement, look backward and forward across actions and label the relationship and its strength.
4. **Quantifying contribution.** Turn all of that into mass scores per party.

Step 4 of this walkthrough covers how your version of each stage works in detail.

### The findings

Applied to 638 real collaboration logs:

- **Humans hold 75 to 89 percent of SHAPER mass. LLMs hold 96 to 99 percent of EXECUTOR mass.** Humans set direction, models shape specifics.
- **LLM goal-shaping rises as goals get more specific**, and is stronger in technical, closed-ended tasks like programming and data analysis than in open-ended ones like writing and planning.
- **Goal shaping is co-constructed**, not user-driven alone. Indirect influence is common.
- Eleven recurring indirect-influence patterns across four categories: underspecified intent, artifact-triggered elaboration, problem-triggered revision, interactional steering.
- **Interaction design changes AI initiative measurably.** Requiring the AI to communicate before acting nearly doubles its goal-shaping, from 24.5 percent to 42.9 percent. Underspecified prompts push AI contribution from 30.65 percent to 69.64 percent.
- **More goal-shaping does not clearly improve output quality.** Pearson correlation of roughly minus 0.002.

That last one is worth pausing on. It means the panel cannot honestly tell anyone that a higher human percentage produces better work. Whatever the panel is for, it is not for optimising quality.

### The user study, which is the actual design brief

Ten participants were shown COTRACE's analysis of their own collaborations.

- Exposure **shifted perceived contribution by about 2 points on a 5-point scale**. Participants rated their own execution contribution roughly 1.8 points lower after seeing the analysis.
- **Nine out of ten** said the tool helped them notice things they had not been aware of.
- **P1:** "It was surprising how much the tool was making decisions without me explicitly stating them."
- **P6:** "although I agree with the final outputs, I didn't necessarily make the micro decisions."
- **P2:** "I feel like I should be way more specific in my prompting."

P6's sentence is your essay, written by a stranger. That is the empirical validation the other three ideas never had.

### The three complaints that are your design brief

This is the most important paragraph in this entire walkthrough.

- **P8: "The tool said I did nothing... I guess it doesn't see the cognitive work of choosing between the items."**
- **P7:** was confused about how the percentages were calculated at a granular level.
- **P6:** was not always convinced the indirect influence the tool flagged was actually meaningful.

Read as a set, they say three separate things:

1. Automatic measurement is **blind to evaluation work**. Choosing, comparing and rejecting leave no artifact trace, so a scorer that reads outputs will tell a thinking person they contributed nothing.
2. A contribution number is **illegible without its evidence**. A percentage the user cannot drill into is not information, it is a verdict.
3. Attribution claims must be **falsifiable by the user**. If the tool asserts an influence the user does not recognise, and the user cannot contest it, the tool loses trust.

Every major design decision in the project traces to one of those three. Live rather than post-hoc, drillable evidence rather than bare numbers, and user marking rather than pure automation. When you redesign the presentation layer, these three are the acceptance test.

There is also a standing reading rule from the earlier sessions, which still applies: **read COTRACE for the problem, not the answer.** Their findings and limitations before designing, their UI figures only after you have sketched your own.

## 2.4 Layer 4: the Five Paradoxes

**Salma, Hijón-Neira and Pizarro, "Designing Co-Creative Systems: Five Paradoxes in Human–AI Collaboration," *Information* 2025, 16, 909, MDPI, published 17 October 2025.** In your files as `CoCreative_Systems_Paradoxes.pdf`, also a layered export.

Their argument is that current tools operate as linear executors of commands, which clashes with the non-linear, iterative and ambiguous nature of human creativity. They propose five tensions that are **irreducible**, meaning they should be treated as design drivers rather than problems to be solved.

Here is their own summary table, in their terms:

| Paradox | Core tension | Their design goal |
|---|---|---|
| **Ambiguity vs. Precision** | Vague human intent against the AI's need for clear input | Translate vision into prompts without limiting exploration |
| **Control vs. Serendipity** | Human direction against the value of unexpected AI discoveries | Enable beneficial accidents while ensuring human authorship |
| **Speed vs. Reflection** | Rapid generation against the need for human critical thought | Use AI for efficiency without causing cognitive deskilling |
| **Individual vs. Collective** | The creator's unique voice against the AI's data-driven wisdom of the crowd | Leverage collective patterns without suppressing individual style |
| **Originality vs. Remix** | The desire for novelty against the AI's recombinative nature | Frame originality as emerging from human curation of the AI's remix |

Two of these deserve extra attention because they connect directly to work you have already done.

**Ambiguity vs. Precision** contains a question the paper poses and does not answer: *determining the source of creativity, whether the human, the AI, or the cooperation itself, is the main challenge.* That is the question COTRACE attacks with measurement and the question your panel attacks with display. This is the paradox your project has the most direct claim on.

**Individual vs. Collective** is your essay's "average of everything" argument, arriving from a completely different direction and published independently. Worth noting that the essay got there first, from observation.

**Speed vs. Reflection** is explicitly about deskilling, so it maps onto the course itself.

A previous session assessed the project against all five honestly and concluded that Ambiguity vs. Precision and Control vs. Serendipity are the two most directly addressed, and the others remain open. That assessment is on the record and the thesis write-up is expected to make this mapping explicit.

## 2.7 The friction literature, and why the nag still lost

Idea 1 was killed for being a nag, but the research behind designed friction is sound and you should keep it, because it explains what a *good* intervention looks like.

## 3.3 The three structural principles

Everything else in the design follows from three rules. If you only retain three things from this step, retain these.

### Principle 1: A mirror, not a judge

From PANEL_SPEC:

> Every element states a fact traceable through the backend to a verbatim quote, and no element praises or shames any way of working.

This is the cardinal rule and it is doing real work. The panel never says you should drive more. It never says the AI is doing too much. If you are on autopilot, it shows autopilot, neutrally, with the same visual weight as any other mode.

Three separate justifications converge here:

- **From Step 1**: the pause-nag idea was killed for preaching. The mirror rule is what stops the panel from quietly becoming the nag again.
- **From Step 2**: the Drosos finding that nudges stop working once they feel like assignments.
- **From Step 2's COTRACE study**: P8 was told they did nothing. That was a verdict. Verdicts wound.

There is a design consequence people miss. **The realisation has to be produced by the user, not delivered by the panel.** That means the panel has to be interesting enough to look at without being told to look at it, and honest enough that when it shows something uncomfortable you believe it. That is a hard bar, and it is the bar.

### Principle 2: Every number traces to evidence

Nothing on screen is decorative or approximate. The chain runs: verbatim quote in the transcript → extracted action → mapped requirement → influence label with a weight → mass score → the number you see.

Each link is inspectable in both directions. You can click a number and walk back to the quote.

This exists because of P7, who could not understand how the percentages were computed, and P6, who did not believe some of the influences the tool claimed. A percentage without its evidence is an assertion. With its evidence it becomes a claim you can check and, importantly, disagree with.

There is a quieter consequence: **it forbids you from inventing display values.** Any visual you design later has to be derivable from the ledger. A shape that looks good but cannot be traced to evidence violates the principle, no matter how nice it is.

### Principle 3: The pair is the universal coordinate

A **pair** is one user message plus one AI reply. P1, P2, P3, and so on.

Every section renders **as of** a pair. The panel is not five independent widgets, it is five views of one shared position. Click a pair anywhere, in the timeline, in the transcript, and all five sections recompute to show the state at that moment.

This is the single most consequential architectural decision in the project. It gives you one state variable to reason about, it makes the whole panel scrubbable through history, and it means live is just the special case where the current pair is the newest one.

Step 6 covers the full model, including what happens when you are scrubbing history and a new reply arrives.

## 3.5 The WHAT axis and the HOW axis

This is where the intellectual contribution sits, so read it slowly.

Sections 2 and 3, Direction and Decisions, answer **WHAT**: who shaped the content of the work, which goals and which requirements.

Section 5 answers **HOW**: what the working relationship looks like, structurally.

These come apart, and the fact that they come apart is the insight. You can shape very little of the WHAT while being fully engaged in the HOW. You can also shape a lot of the WHAT while being entirely disengaged, by firing off specifications and accepting everything back without reading.

COTRACE only measures the WHAT. BCG only describes the HOW. The proposal that the two form two axes of one space, that the BCG archetypes are the macro pattern and COTRACE's action labels are the micro mechanics underneath, was worked out in this project and is not in either source. # STEP 4 — The Measurement Core

## What this step is and why it is the heaviest

This is the engine. Everything you saw in Step 3 is a rendering of what this step produces.

Three reasons it matters more than the others.

**It is the part that is genuinely hard.** The UI can be rebuilt in a week. This pipeline took months of specification and is now on version 5. It is also the part that decides whether the whole product is honest, because if the numbers are wrong the panel is a confident lie.

**It is the part your new idea would sit on.** Your brain-map concept takes the same extraction and represents it differently. To know whether any representation is possible, you need to know exactly what the engine emits, in what shape, and when. That is this step.

**It is where the project currently stands.** Phase 2 is the engine phase, and it is the active phase. Understanding this is understanding your next working day.

---

## 4.0 The one governing idea

From your architecture doc:

> The pipeline engine consumes "pair events" and does not know where they come from.

The engine receives a pair, one user message plus one AI reply, and analyses it. It does not know or care whether that pair arrived from a live chat or from a replayed export file.

This single decision is why the build is possible at all. It lets you develop and test the entire engine offline against a frozen fixture, months before any live chat exists. It is also why replay survives as a test harness after the v1.2 correction demoted it as a product.

Keep this in mind: **the engine is a pure function of the pair sequence.** Same pairs in, same analysis out, in principle. In practice the LLM introduces variance, which is section 4.6.

---

## 4.1 The vocabulary

Six terms. Everything in the pipeline is one of these, and you cannot read the spec or the code without them.

**Action.** An atomic thing one party did in one turn. A single message contains several. "Build me a login page, use Tailwind, and keep it minimal" is not one action, it is three. Each action gets a role, SHAPER or EXECUTOR, from the COTRACE framework in Step 2.

**Outcome.** The thing being worked toward. Outcomes are the nodes of the goal tree: a root goal, its children, their children. R0 is the root, and renaming the chat renames R0, which tells you the goal tree and the chat title are the same object.

**Requirement.** The smallest verifiable success predicate. Something you can check true or false against the output. "The page must use Tailwind" is a requirement. "Make it good" is not, because nothing can verify it. The fixture contains **14 distinct requirements** at pair 1.

**Slot.** A requirement-shaped hole that has been opened but not yet filled. Somebody said the thing needs a colour scheme but nobody has said which one. Slots are how the engine represents work that is pending rather than decided. They have age counters, and there is a three-pair abandonment sweep, so a slot nobody fills within three pairs is closed as abandoned rather than hanging forever.

**Influence label.** A claim that a particular action affected a particular requirement, with a type and a strength. This is where direct goal shaping and indirect influence from Step 2 live. Each label is one row in the ledger.

**Mass.** The accumulated weight of influence attributed to one party. Δ_you and Δ_AI. In the fixture, **87.0 and 314.0**, which produce the 21.7 / 78.3 split.

The chain, in one line:

**quote → action → outcome → requirement (or slot) → influence label → ledger row → mass → panel number**

That chain is Principle 2 from Step 3, made mechanical. Every arrow is inspectable in both directions, which is what makes the panel drillable and what answers P7 and P6 from Step 2.

---

## 4.2 The pipeline, stage by stage

Six stages. The first five call an LLM. The last one is pure arithmetic with no AI in it at all, which is deliberate: the numbers on screen come from Python you can read, not from a model you have to trust.

```
Pair arrives
  → Step 1a  extract actions
  → Step 1b  map actions to outcomes / goal tree
  → Step 1c  identify intentions
  → Step 2   extract requirements per outcome
  → Step 3   score influence per requirement
  → Stage 4  pure math, produces every panel number
```

### Step 1a: extract actions

Takes the raw pair. Splits each message into atomic actions and tags each with its role, SHAPER or EXECUTOR.

Everything downstream is built on this decomposition, so the whole pipeline's accuracy is capped here. Split too coarsely and you lose decisions. Split too finely and you inflate one sentence into five decisions and the counts stop meaning anything.

### Step 1b: map actions to outcomes

Places each action on the goal tree. Does it belong to an existing goal, does it open a new child goal, or does it modify the structure itself?

Two mechanisms here that SPEC_QUESTIONS Q3 exposes:

- An **action_to_outcome mapping** is produced and carried forward, because Step 2 uses it as a per-outcome filter. Step 2 does not look at every action for every outcome, only the ones 1b assigned there.
- A **rolling dialogue_summary** is maintained, used for what the spec calls SELF-REFERENCE. This is how the engine keeps context across pairs without re-reading the whole transcript on every turn.

Both of these are genuinely stateful. They cannot be recomputed from scratch, which is exactly the problem Q3 was written about, and why they now live in `run/pipeline_state.json` outside the frozen contracts.

### Step 1c: identify intentions

The layer between an action and a requirement. What was the party trying to achieve with that action, as distinct from what they literally said. This is the bridge that makes indirect influence detectable: an action that supplies context without stating a requirement still carries an intention, and that intention is what later motivates a requirement.

### Step 2: extract requirements per outcome

For each outcome, using only the actions 1b assigned to it, pull out the binary-testable requirements. Also opens slots where a requirement is implied but unspecified.

The per-outcome filter is a cost and accuracy decision: it keeps each LLM call small and focused rather than asking one call to reason over the entire conversation.

### Step 3: score influence per requirement

The heart of the measurement. For each requirement, look across actions and label which ones influenced it, of what type, at what strength. Each label becomes a ledger row. The fixture's ledger is **157 rows** for 14 requirements, which tells you the average requirement carries around eleven influence claims. Influence is not one-to-one, it is dense.

This step is where the thirteen influence subtypes and the E1 and E2 extractors named in AGENTS.md live. **The exact subtype list and the weight attached to each one are in COTRACE_PIPELINE_SPEC and I do not have them.** That is the single biggest gap in my current picture of your engine, and it is the part that most directly determines whether 87.0 and 314.0 come out right.

### Stage 4: the math

No LLM. Reads the ledger, aggregates, and emits every number the panel shows. Section 4.4 covers what it produces.

---

## 4.3 The iteration mechanism

This is the part most people miss, and it is what makes the analysis *live* rather than merely incremental.

A naive version would analyse pair 5 and leave pairs 1 through 4 alone. That would be wrong, because **later turns change the meaning of earlier ones.** You say something vague at pair 2, and at pair 7 it becomes clear what you meant. The influence existed at pair 2. It only became visible at pair 7.

So the engine re-opens earlier work. From what SPEC_QUESTIONS Q3 exposes, there are two triggers, and Trigger B works like this: for each requirement, the engine tracks which action IDs have already been labelled against it, and on re-analysis it sends **only the new subsequent actions**. It does not re-score what it already scored. That is both a cost control and a stability control, because re-scoring old pairs from scratch would make your numbers jitter for no reason.

Slots have their own lifecycle, with age counters and the three-pair abandonment sweep mentioned above.

**Trigger A and B, the full iteration mechanism, and the abandonment rules are spec §9.** I know their shape, not their exact conditions.

Two consequences worth holding:

1. **The panel's history is not frozen.** A number shown at pair 3 can legitimately change when you reach pair 7, because the evidence for it changed. Any design that assumes past pairs are immutable is designing against the engine.
2. **This is what makes the goal tree grow rather than just extend.** Structure gets revised, not only appended.

## 4.4 What Stage 4 produces, number by number

Using the fixture, which AGENTS.md rule 5 declares sacred.

### Direction: You 21.7 percent / AI 78.3 percent

From **Δ_you = 87.0** and **Δ_AI = 314.0**. Total 401.0. 87 / 401 = 21.7 percent.

These are weighted sums over ledger rows: every influence claim contributes its weight to whichever party's action produced it. So Direction is not a count of messages, not a count of words, and not a count of decisions. It is accumulated influence mass.

Note the shape of it: the AI's 314 comes largely from many small influence claims, since it produces most of the actions. A single decisive human sentence and forty small AI elaborations can produce exactly this kind of split, and that is the honest reading of the number rather than a flaw in it.

### Decisions: 4 you, 10 AI

A **creator split**: for each of the 14 distinct requirements, who introduced it. Four were yours, ten were the AI's. The Phase 0 test explicitly checks 14 distinct requirements, zero overlap and no duplicate rows, which tells you this is a clean partition.

Direction and Decisions measure different things from the same data. Direction weights all influence; Decisions counts only origination. That is why they can diverge, and the fact that they roughly agree here, 21.7 percent against 4/14 at 28.6 percent, is a mild sanity signal rather than a coincidence.

### Mode: COPILOT, with w = 4/10 and h = 47.0 / 239.0

Two ratios, not one.

- **w = 4/10.** The 4 and 10 are the decision counts. So w is the WHAT ratio, expressed as your decisions against the AI's.
- **h = 47.0 / 239.0.** Different scale, roughly 0.197. These numbers are smaller than 87.0 and 314.0, so h is computed over a **subset** of the ledger, not all of it. My read is that h is the HOW ratio over some restricted class of influence, execution-side or a particular subtype group, but **which subset is spec §10 and I cannot verify it.** Flag this for the pipeline spec.

The mode then falls out of where the pair (w, h) lands against thresholds. This is the WHAT and HOW two-axis structure from Step 3, computed.

And this is the exact place where the Step 3 caveat bites: **those thresholds are your judgement call, not COTRACE's finding.** The WHAT numbers inherit a validated method. The mode boundaries were chosen in this project. Phase 5 is named for calibration and its Definition of Done is a complete CALIBRATION.md, which tells you this was recognised and deferred rather than forgotten.

## 4.5 The five artifacts

The engine's entire output surface. One folder per chat.

| File | What it holds | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `dialogue.json` | The conversation turns | The input |
| `state.json` | Actions, outcomes, requirements, slots | The current understanding |
| `ledger.jsonl` | One influence claim per line, append-only, 157 rows in the fixture | The evidence |
| `snapshots.json` | Per-pair cumulative scores | The history, pair by pair |
| `panel_bundle.json` | Pre-computed panel data | What the UI reads |

Four properties worth noticing, because they constrain any redesign:

- **The ledger is append-only JSONL.** Evidence accumulates and is never rewritten. That is what makes the audit trail trustworthy.
- **snapshots.json is why scrubbing works.** Cumulative scores are stored per pair, so showing the panel "as of P4" is a lookup rather than a recomputation. Your Step 3 pair coordinate is implemented here.
- **panel_bundle.json is the contract with the frontend**, and decision D13 says the frontend does zero math. Every provenance decision lives in one tested Python place.

That third point has a direct bearing on your new idea. **Any new visualisation has to be fed by panel_bundle.json**, or panel_bundle has to grow, which is a spec amendment at the command centre rather than a frontend change. A graph view needs nodes and edges. Whether the current bundle carries enough structure to draw them is a concrete, answerable question, and it is one of the first things worth checking when you get to designing.

## 4.6 Honesty, and the non-determinism problem

Spec §12 is called the honesty ledger, and §12.9 documents LLM non-determinism.

Your own COMPARISON.md is the live evidence:

| Metric | Live run, pair 1 | Canonical fixture, pair 1 |
|---|---|---|
| Requirement count | 1 | 14 |
| Direction split | You 33.3 / AI 66.7 | You 21.7 / AI 78.3 |
| Usage mode | COPILOT | COPILOT |

Read that carefully, because it is the most important status fact in the whole build.

The file notes that differences are expected under non-determinism. That is true for the split. **It does not explain 1 requirement against 14.** That is not variance, that is a different order of magnitude. Either the smoke test ran on a truncated input, or extraction under the current model configuration is finding almost nothing.

This matters because of Phase 2's Definition of Done, which is fixture regression **EXACT**. A pipeline producing 1 requirement where the fixture has 14 does not pass that gate. So the gap between where the build is and where the gate is may be larger than the phase status line suggests.

I am flagging this rather than diagnosing it. Diagnosing it is a working session, not a teaching step. But when you open the repo again, this is the first thing worth looking at, and it is a plausible candidate for why the work stopped in July.

There is a plausible link to the Gemini switch in Q1: the extraction prompts were written and verified against one model family and the engine now runs on another, with a flash-lite model on the fast path. Prompts are copied verbatim from the spec and never "improved", which is the right rule, but verbatim prompts on a different model can behave differently. That is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion.

---

## 4.7 The honest limits of the measurement

Four things the engine cannot do, each of which is a design constraint rather than a bug.

1. **It is blind to evaluation work.** P8's complaint from Step 2. Choosing between options, rejecting, judging: none of it produces a requirement, so none of it produces mass. The engine will always under-count a thoughtful reader. This is the deepest unsolved problem in the project, and it is not solvable inside the pipeline. It needs the user to be able to mark, which is why user marking was in the Idea 4 origin note from Step 1.
2. **It costs five to twenty seconds per pair.** Turned into a feature by the loading treatment, which signals that the panel is thinking too, but it is a real constraint on any live design.
3. **It is stochastic.** Same conversation, different run, different numbers. §12.9 acknowledges this. A panel presenting stochastic output with two decimal places is making an implicit precision claim it cannot support.
4. **It cannot tell you whether the work is good.** COTRACE's own near-zero correlation from Step 2. The engine measures shaping, not quality.

## 5.1 §0, the vocabulary law

Before any element is described, the spec constrains the words. Four rules.

**"Decisions" not "requirements."** The backend word is requirement. The screen word is decision. Requirement is engineering vocabulary and it sounds like a specification document. Decision is what the thing actually was: a moment where the work could have gone two ways and went one. It is also the word that makes P6's complaint from Step 2 land. "I didn't make the micro decisions" is a sentence about decisions, not requirements.

**"Open questions" not "open slots."** Same move. A slot is a data structure. An open question is a thing you recognise from your own working life.

**"You / AI" not "user / assistant."** User is what a system calls you. You is what you call yourself. This is the difference between being described and being addressed, and it matters enormously for a tool whose whole job is showing you yourself.

**No textual state labels.** No "MAIN GOAL", no "CURRENT", no "NOW". The spec's reason is exact: position and emphasis carry meaning, and words never restate what the visual already says.

That fourth rule is the strongest design principle in the document and it is worth generalising. It says the layout must be legible without captions. If you need to write "CURRENT" next to something, your emphasis has failed and the label is patching it. This is also a direct answer to the course's requirement 6 from Step 1, understandable without verbal explanation, applied at the element level.

Every one of these four is a **restatement of the mirror rule at the level of language.** Engineering vocabulary makes a person feel measured by a system. Plain vocabulary makes them feel shown something about themselves.

---

## 5.2 The colour law

Two colours, fixed, and the Build Playbook calls them law:

- **Blue `#0057FF` = you, always left**
- **Orange `#E85A0A` = AI, always right**

They exist as CSS variables `--you` and `--ai` and are never hardcoded anywhere.

Three things to notice.

**Side is part of the meaning.** You are always left, the AI is always right. Once that holds everywhere, a person reads the split bar preattentively, without parsing the numbers. Consistency of position is doing as much work as the colour.

**Blue and orange are complementary and roughly equal in visual weight.** Neither reads as the good one. Compare what green and red would have done to the same bar. This is the mirror rule at the level of palette.

**Two colours only, for sides.** Grey is available for a third state, and the timeline uses it, but there is no fourth party colour. That is a real constraint on any redesign, because the moment you have more than two entities you are outside the current colour system.

## 5.3 §1, the GOAL section

The mechanism is called **thread-collapse**, and the spec's own reference is YouTube comment threads.

Default view, top to bottom:

```
main goal
⌄ N more
previous goal
current goal        (emphasised)
```

You always see the root, you always see where you are, you see the one step above you, and everything in between collapses into a chip that tells you how much is hidden.

**Depth cases d=0, d=1, d=2, d≥3 are each specified separately.** That is more care than it looks. At depth 0 there is only a root and no collapse is possible. At depth 1 and 2 the full chain fits and the chip should not appear at all. Only at depth 3 or more does collapse engage. Specifying each case separately is what stops the "⌄ 0 more" bug that this kind of component always ships with.

**Expansion is progressive, one segment at a time, never an all-at-once dump.** Clicking the chip does not explode the whole tree. It reveals the next level. This is the same instinct as thread-collapse itself: keep the reader oriented, never hand them a wall.

Why this design at all: the goal tree can get deep, and a full tree view would make the panel about the tree rather than about you. Thread-collapse keeps the section answering its actual question from Step 3, *where am I in my own work right now*, rather than becoming a file browser.

**The readouts.** `You — 59%` and `AI — 41%`.

## 5.6 §4, the TIMELINE section

The spec calls this the most complex section, and it has two states.

### Collapsed row

Four elements per pair:

1. **Pair label.** P1, P2, P3.
2. **Turn-delta micro-spine.** A tiny visual of how much changed in this exchange. It lets you scan the column and see where the heavy turns were without opening anything.
3. **Summary line, five words maximum.**

- **Orange** = AI-created
- **Grey** = straddling

# STEP 6 — The Interaction Model

## What this step is and why it matters

PANEL_SPEC said what renders. This says how it behaves. INTERACTION_SPEC v1, 167 lines, the smallest of the four documents and in some ways the most elegant.

Three reasons to take it seriously.

**It contains the project's cleanest piece of design reasoning.** The whole interactive surface reduces to one primitive. Most interfaces accumulate interaction types until nobody can hold the model in their head. This one refused to.

**It is what makes "live" actually work.** Step 3 told you live was the special case where the viewed pair is the newest one. This is where that claim gets cashed out, including what happens when you are reading history and a new reply lands.

**It is the layer most people forget to redesign.** A new visual form inherits none of these rules automatically. If you change the representation, every rule below has to be re-answered for the new form, and the questions themselves are the valuable part, not the current answers.

## 6.1 §0, the one interaction model

The governing sentence:

> Every interactive element either **sets** the viewed pair, or **renders as of** the viewed pair. There are no other interaction primitives.

Read that again, because it is stronger than it looks. It is not a description, it is a prohibition. There is no third kind of interaction. No element that filters. No element that toggles a display option. No element with its own local state. Everything is one of two things.

What this buys you:

- **One state variable.** The viewed pair. That is the entire interactive state of the panel.
- **Consistency for free.** If all five sections render as of the viewed pair, they cannot disagree. You do not need to keep them in sync because they are reading the same number.
- **A learnable model.** The user learns one rule, clicking a thing moves you to a moment, and it applies everywhere.

This is the pair coordinate from Step 3 promoted from a data concept to an interaction law. It is also the single most portable idea in the entire project. Whatever form the panel takes, this rule can survive intact, and it is the kind of thing that is very hard to invent twice.

---

## 6.2 The two global states

| State | Meaning | Indicator |
|---|---|---|
| **LIVE** | Viewed pair = latest pair. The panel updates as the conversation moves. | Green `LIVE` pill |
| **HISTORY** | Viewed pair < latest. The panel is frozen at that moment. | Amber `● VIEWING Pn · HISTORY` |

Two rules attached.

**The state shows once, in the top strip.** Never repeated per row, per section, or per message.

That rule is §0's no-textual-labels principle from Step 5 applied to state. The temptation in a panel like this is enormous: dim every section, badge every row, add "historical" captions everywhere. The spec forbids it. One indicator, one place, and the rest of the panel is trusted to be read correctly because the user knows where they are.

**Colour carries the distinction.** Green for live, amber for history. Amber is the right choice and worth noticing: red would say error, grey would say disabled. Amber says *elsewhere*. You are not broken and you are not stuck, you are looking at another moment. And note it does not collide with the blue and orange side colours, so state and attribution never compete visually.

---

## 6.3 §3, the five scrub sources

Scrub means changing the viewed pair. There are exactly five ways:

1. **Timeline row click.** Scrub to that pair. The obvious one.
2. **Timeline drawer expand.** Expanding *is* scrubbing. Opening a pair's drawer moves you to that pair.
3. **Goal-node click.** Scrub to that node's first-appearance pair. Clicking a goal takes you to the moment that goal appeared.
4. **Decisions latest-example tap.** Scrub to that decision's creation pair. Tap the example sentence and you are standing at the moment it was decided.
5. **Back-to-latest.** Return to LIVE.

Sources 3 and 4 are the interesting ones, because they turn the panel into a set of doorways rather than a set of readouts. Every noun on the screen is a link to when it happened. That is Principle 2 from Step 3 made navigable: evidence is not just attached to numbers, it is reachable from them.

Source 2 is a small, clever collapse. It could have been two separate actions, expanding and scrubbing. Making expansion imply scrubbing removes a whole class of confusing state where you are viewing P3 with P7's drawer open.

## 6.4 The rule that scroll is never scrub

> Scrolling the chat does NOT change the viewed pair. Only explicit clicks do.

This is the most important rule in the document and it is easy to underrate.

The obvious design is scroll-linking: as you scroll the transcript, the panel follows along. It feels magical in a demo. It is wrong here, for two reasons.

**It makes the panel jittery and unreadable.** Numbers changing under your eyes while you are trying to read them. You could never hold a value still long enough to think about it.

**It removes intent.** Scrolling is ambient and half-conscious. Clicking is deliberate. If the panel moved when you scrolled, you would never know whether you chose to be at P4 or drifted there. And this is a tool whose entire purpose is helping you notice what you chose versus what happened to you. A panel that quietly relocates you while you scroll would be enacting the exact failure it exists to reveal.

That is the rule's real justification, and it is a good example of the thesis reaching down into a small UI decision.

1. User hits Enter

2. Server streams the reply over SSE

3. On reply completion, server enqueues the pipeline job for pair t

   → Rail shows loading treatment, previous values STAY on screen

4. Engine runs 1a → 1b → 1c → 2 → 3 → Stage 4

5. SSE "pair_ready t"
   → Frontend fetches the updated bundle, sections update atomically
   → New timeline row appears, counters increment

6. If the user was in HISTORY, nothing yanks them

## What this step is and why it comes here

Steps 4, 5 and 6 covered the three specs that say what the system does, shows and how it behaves. This step covers the fourth: ARCHITECTURE v1.3, which says how it is built and in what order.

Two reasons it matters.

**It is the bridge between design and reality.** A design is a wish until something decides the stack, the boundaries and the sequence. The thirteen decisions are where those wishes got resolved, each with a rationale. Knowing the rationale is what lets you tell a real constraint from an arbitrary one, which is exactly the judgement a redesign needs.

**It is your map back to work.** The phase plan says what is done, what is next, and what gate stands between them. When you close this walkthrough and open the repo, this is the document that tells you where to stand.

---

## 7.1 The governing idea, restated

> The pipeline engine consumes pair events and does not know where they come from.

One sentence, and most of the architecture follows from it. Because the engine is source-agnostic, the build can be sequenced backwards from the user: engine first against a fixture, then server, then live chat. That is why the phase order is possible at all.

---

## 7.2 The four layers

| Layer | What it is | Its job | Location |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Web app, React + TypeScript + Vite + Zustand | The eyes. Renders everything. Zero math. | `web/` |
| 2 | Server, FastAPI, async | Traffic control. Manages chats, streams replies, triggers the engine, pushes updates. | `server/` |
| 3 | Engine, pure Python | The brain. The COTRACE pipeline. | `engine/` |
| 4 | Artifact store, JSON files | The memory. One folder per chat. | `data/chats/<chat_id>/` |

The layout is three columns: sidebar 240px, chat flexible, right rail 360px.

Two boundaries are load-bearing, not incidental.

**Between 1 and 2 there is no shared logic.** The frontend reads `panel_bundle.json` and `dialogue.json`. That is the entire surface. Nothing else crosses.

**Between 3 and 4 the files are the interface.** The engine does not hand objects to the server. It writes artifacts, and the server reads them. That is why a crashed run leaves valid files or no files, and why you can debug the whole system with a text editor.

| # | Decision | Choice | Rationale |

| D2 | Engine language | Python | Ecosystem, plus your existing scripts |

| D6 | Storage | Files, no database | Debuggable, git-diffable, single-user |

## 7.4 The API surface

Six endpoints. That is the entire server.

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /chats` | List chats, for the sidebar |
| `POST /chats` | Create a chat, meaning a new folder on disk |
| `POST /chats/{id}/messages` | Send a message, AI reply streams back |
| `GET /chats/{id}/bundle` | Full panel bundle plus dialogue, for initial load |
| `GET /chats/{id}/events` | SSE stream for `pair_ready` and `pipeline_status` |
| `PATCH /chats/{id}/title` | Rename the chat, which renames the root goal node R0 |

The last one is the interesting one. **Renaming a chat renames R0.** The chat title and the root of the goal tree are the same object. # Testing the engine on real data, and how it folds into the build

## Part 1: The core problem, and the move that solves it

You named the real difficulty yourself. The pipeline calls an LLM five times per pair, so you cannot write a test that says "this chat must produce 14 requirements." Run it again tomorrow and you get 12. That is not a bug, and chasing exact values on LLM output is how people waste months.

The move is to **stop testing values and start testing properties.**

Three tiers, and every piece of the engine falls into exactly one:

| Tier | What it covers | Standard | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Exact** | Everything with no LLM in the path: Stage 4a maths, projections, state transitions, schema validation, mode classifier, R-SUM | Byte-exact. The canonical numbers must come out every time. | Under a second |
| **2. Invariant** | The LLM half, run on real chats | The output varies. The listed properties must hold on every run, on every chat. | Minutes |
| **3. Robustness** | Scale, volume, malformed input, failure injection | Does not check correctness. Checks that it does not fall over, leak, hang or corrupt. | Slow, run on demand |

Tier 1 is where certainty lives, and it is most of your real coverage. Tier 2 is where real chats live, and it is the answer to "is the engine actually working." Tier 3 is the answer to your worry about too much data and unusual situations.

There is also a **Tier 0, replay**: record LLM responses once, commit them, replay them in tests. Same tests as Tier 2 but deterministic and free, so they can run on every commit. Tier 2 against the live API runs weekly or at a phase gate.

---

## Part 2: The corpus

This is preparation work and it should happen before any engine code is written, because everything downstream tests against it.

### What it is

A folder of real exported chats, each with a metadata file describing what it is and what you expect from it. You already have ten reference chats in `docs/Reference chats/`, so this is largely a classification job rather than a collection job.

```
data/corpus/
  manifest.json                  ← index of every chat with its attributes
  c01_coding_short/
    source.json                  ← the raw export, untouched
    dialogue.json                ← normalised into engine format
    meta.yaml                    ← what this chat is and what to expect
  c02_writing_long/
  ...
  golden_01/                     ← the one hand-labelled chat
    dialogue.json
    expected.md                  ← your hand analysis of pairs 1 to 3
```

### The coverage matrix

Ten chats is the right number. Aim for one chat in each cell rather than ten of the same kind. The dimensions that actually change engine behaviour:

| Dimension | Values to cover | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Length** | short 3 to 5 pairs, medium 10 to 20, long 40+ | Long chats grow the accumulate window, raise cost, stress Trigger B |
| **Task type** | coding, writing, planning, research, creative, debugging | COTRACE found technical closed-ended tasks produce more AI goal-shaping than open-ended ones. Your engine should reproduce that. |
| **Prompt style** | highly specified, versus vague one-liners | COTRACE found underspecified prompts move AI share from 30.65% to 69.64%. This is your strongest sanity check. |
| **Expected mode** | one chat you know is you-driving, one copilot, one autopilot | Gives the mode classifier something real to be judged against |
| **Awkward content** | code blocks, non-English, a 3000-word single message, lists, attachments | Extraction breakers |

### `meta.yaml` per chat

```yaml
id: c01_coding_short
source: claude_export
pairs: 4
task_type: coding
prompt_style: specified
language: en
contains: [code_blocks]
expected:
  mode_hint: centaur          # your judgement, not a hard assertion
  direction_hint: user_heavy  # user_heavy | balanced | ai_heavy
  min_requirements: 2
  max_requirements: 20
notes: "User gave full spec up front, AI mostly executed."
```

The `expected` block is deliberately soft. `direction_hint` is not "21.7%", it is "the user should come out heavier than the AI here." If a chat where you dictated everything comes back as 90% AI, something is broken, and that is a test you can write without pretending to know the exact number.

### The golden chat

One short chat, three pairs, where **you personally** write out every action, requirement and attribution by hand before running the engine. That becomes fixture two, the extraction fixture, alongside your existing fixture one, the maths fixture. Fixture one has no dialogue text and tests Stage 4a. Fixture two has real text and tests extraction. Two fixtures, two jobs, neither replaces the other.

This is a few hours of tedious work and it is the highest-value few hours in the whole rebuild, because it is the only ground truth you will ever have about whether extraction is any good.

---

## Part 3: The invariant catalogue

These are the assertions that must hold on every chat, every run, forever. They are written once as a shared module and then called from tests, from the CLI and from the live path.

**Referential integrity**
1. Every artifact validates against its schema.
2. Every action id matches `^([UA])\((\d+),(\d+)\)$` and is unique.
3. Every ledger row's `action_id`, `req_id` and `outcome_id` exist in state.
4. Every action maps to exactly one outcome.
5. No duplicate ledger rows on `(action_id, req_id, pair_added, kind)`.

**Structure**
6. The outcome tree has exactly one root, no cycles, every parent exists, and `children[]` agrees with `parent` pointers in both directions.
7. Every requirement has at least one creation action.
8. Every requirement's `created_at_pair` is less than or equal to the current pair.
9. Slot status is one of open, resolved, abandoned. A resolved slot links to a requirement. An abandoned slot has been inactive for at least three pairs.

**Arithmetic**
10. All scores are finite and positive.
11. The sum of per-pair deltas equals the cumulative total at the final pair.
12. Creator counts sum to the number of distinct requirements.
13. Cumulative mass is monotonically non-decreasing across pairs.
14. `h_you ≤ delta_you` and `h_ai ≤ delta_ai`, because SHAPER scores are a subset of all scores. If this ever fails, the definition has drifted.
15. Percentages are in [0, 100] and sum to 100 within rounding.
16. The mode is a pure function of `w` and `h` and is one of the four values.

**Process**
17. **Append-only holds.** Ledger rows for pair `t` are unchanged after pair `t+1` is processed, unless an explicit rerun wipes them.
18. **Idempotency.** Rerunning pair `t` twice leaves the same ledger state as running it once.
19. **Determinism of the pure half.** The same ledger in produces byte-identical `analysis.json` out.
20. **Batch equals live.** The same chat through both entry points, with cached LLM responses, produces identical ledgers. This is the single most important test in your whole suite, because it is what makes the two modes one engine rather than two.

Invariant 20 is the one that guarantees the property you asked me about at the start.

---

## Part 4: The non-determinism question, answered properly

Rather than treating variance as an unknown, **measure it and publish it**.

Pick three corpus chats. Run each five times against the live API. Record:

| Metric | What to record |
|---|---|
| Requirement count | min, max, mean, coefficient of variation |
| Direction split | spread in percentage points |
| Decision split | spread |
| Mode | how often the mode flips between runs |
| Ledger rows | spread |

Write the result into `docs/STABILITY.md` and amend pipeline spec §12.9 with the real numbers. Then you have a sentence like: *direction varies by plus or minus 4 points across runs, and the mode is stable in 14 of 15 runs.* That is an honest, defensible property of the instrument.

It also has direct thesis value. A panel showing 21.7% when the true figure is 21.7 plus or minus 4 is making a precision claim it cannot support, and knowing the band tells you how many significant figures the interface is allowed to display. That is a design decision you currently cannot make, and this measurement makes it makeable.

The test then becomes: **is the variance within the documented band?** A run that lands outside it is a regression signal. That turns an unknown into a gate.

---

## Part 5: Robustness, your "too much data" worry

This is Tier 3, and it is not about correct numbers. It is about the engine staying standing.

| Scenario | How to test | What must not happen |
|---|---|---|
| Very long chat | 60+ pair chat through batch | Context overflow, quadratic slowdown, memory growth, cost blowup |
| Huge single message | One 20,000-word pair | Prompt exceeds the model window and hard-fails instead of truncating silently |
| Rapid succession, live | Send five messages without waiting | The per-chat lock queues them, no interleaving, no lost pairs |
| Mid-run crash | Kill the process between steps | Resume from `--resume` leaves no half-written artifacts |
| API failure | Inject 500s and timeouts | Four retries with backoff, then a clean failed status, never a corrupt ledger |
| Malformed LLM output | Feed broken JSON through the cache | Repair chain, then a clean hard error, never a silent bad row |
| Empty or trivial pair | "ok" replied with "ok" | Produces a quiet pair, not a crash and not invented requirements |
| Slot churn | A chat where questions open and never resolve | Abandonment sweep fires and slots do not accumulate forever |
| Two chats at once | Run batch on two chats in parallel | D11 says parallelism across chats is free. Prove it. |

Two measurements worth capturing during these runs, because they will decide what is feasible later: **time per pair as a function of pair index**, and **tokens per pair as a function of pair index**. If either curve bends upward, your accumulate windows are growing without bound and long chats will eventually become unusable. Better to know that at pair 60 in a test than at a demo.

---

## Part 6: Bake the checking into the engine itself

This is the part that answers "testing and analysis baked into everything."

Do not leave the invariants only in the test suite. Put them in `engine/checks.py` and run them **after every pipeline run, in production, on every chat**, live or batch.

```
process_pair() → write artifacts → run checks → 
    pass: continue
    fail: write the violation into run/status.json, mark the pair unhealthy
```

The pipeline spec already has §11.4 mechanical checks. This promotes them from a test-time nicety to a runtime guarantee. The effect is that every single run of the engine, forever, verifies itself, and you can never silently accumulate a corrupt ledger.

Alongside it, emit a **run report** per chat:

```
data/chats/<id>/run/report.json
  pairs_processed, wall_time_per_pair[], tokens_per_pair[],
  llm_calls, retries, cache_hits,
  requirements_created, slots_opened/resolved/abandoned,
  checks: {passed: [...], failed: [...]},
  final: {direction, decisions, mode}
```

That file is your instrument panel for the instrument. It is also the raw material for the thesis chapter on how the system performs, and it costs almost nothing to produce.
